explanations.explanation: Outside the camp is right. The person had been living out there alone (Leviticus 13:46), so the priest makes the trip to him. That's a priest who owns comfortable sandals, friend. He doesn't wait for anybody to show up at his door.

A city gate! Friend, I love the confidence. But there's no gate anywhere in this verse. Leviticus 14:3 says, “The priest is to go outside the camp to examine him…” The person had been living outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46), so that's where the priest heads. Picture him walking right past the gate without even slowing down, like a man who knows exactly where he's going and has zero interest in the scenic route.

No mountain here, friend. The verse says the priest is to “…go outside the camp to examine him…” and that's where the person has been staying (Leviticus 13:46). A mountain climb for one inspection would be a LOT of cardio. The priest just heads out past the edge of the camp.

Seven times is right. The text says, “Seven times he shall sprinkle the one to be cleansed of the skin disease.” Keep your eye on that number, because the oil gets sprinkled seven times later (Leviticus 14:16), and so does the house at the end (Leviticus 14:51). The priest isn't winging it with a flick and a shrug.

Close on the count, but it's not three. The verse says “Seven times he shall sprinkle the one to be cleansed of the skin disease.” That's a full seven, no shortcuts. I'd lose count after four, so I respect the priest's focus.

Twelve is a big number, but the text says seven. Leviticus 14:7 reads, “Seven times he shall sprinkle the one to be cleansed of the skin disease.” Seven comes back later in this chapter too, with the oil and with the house. Twelve would be showing off.

True. Right after the seven sprinklings, the text says, “Then he shall pronounce him clean…” (Leviticus 14:7). The priest is the one who says it out loud. That's a word the person has been waiting a long time to hear, I think.

It's true, friend. After the sprinkling, Leviticus 14:7 says the priest “…shall pronounce him clean…” That happens right there, before the live bird is released. The sprinkling comes first and then comes the word.

explanations.answer: It's released into the open field
explanations.explanation: Released into the open field is right. The text says the priest “…shall pronounce him clean and release the live bird into the open field.” No altar for this one. It gets sent off into the open, and I think that bird has earned some sky.

explanations.answer: It's offered up on the altar
explanations.explanation: The altar is a good guess, since offerings come later in this chapter. But for this bird, Leviticus 14:7 says the priest releases it into the open field. The other bird is the one slaughtered. This one gets let go.

explanations.answer: It's given to the priest's family
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this passage sends the bird home with the priest. The verse says he releases the live bird “…into the open field.” No family, no cage, no little bird sweater. It just goes.

Outside his own tent is right. Leviticus 14:8 says, “…he may enter the camp, but he must remain outside his tent for seven days.” He's back in the camp, so that part's a win. But his own front door has to wait a week.

Nope, the priest's tent isn't in this verse. It says the person “…must remain outside his tent for seven days.” His tent, not the priest's. He's back in the camp, and his own tent is the one that matters here.

The Tent of Meeting does show up in this chapter, but not here. Leviticus 14:8 says he “…must remain outside his tent for seven days.” That's his own tent, in the camp he's now allowed to enter. The Tent of Meeting comes into play on the eighth day (Leviticus 14:11).

Water is right. Leviticus 14:9 says, “He must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water, and he will be clean.” Water has already shown up in this passage, since the first bird was slaughtered over fresh water. Plain, simple, and it does the job.

Oil is coming, friend, just not here. This verse says he bathes himself “…with water, and he will be clean.” The olive oil shows up on the eighth day (Leviticus 14:10). Right now the bath is all water.

No wine in this bath. Leviticus 14:9 says he washes his clothes and bathes himself “…with water, and he will be clean.” Wine doesn't appear anywhere in this passage. That's a fancy bath, but not this one.

explanations.answer: At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting
explanations.explanation: At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting is right, friend! Leviticus 14:11 says the priest presents the person with the offerings “…before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” Look at this guy: he's got two lambs, a ewe lamb, flour and oil, and he's standing right there in front of the LORD. I think that's a lot to carry, and I bet he's grinning anyway. Earlier in the passage he's outside the camp, and now here he is at the Tent of Meeting.

explanations.answer: Out in the open field by the camp
explanations.explanation: The open field is where the live bird was released (Leviticus 14:7). Here, the person and his offerings are presented “…at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” Different moment, different spot. Easy to mix up with all this walking around.

explanations.answer: Beside the river outside the camp
explanations.explanation: No river in this scene, friend. The text says the priest presents the person “…before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” Water did show up earlier with the clay pot, which may be the mix-up. This part happens at the Tent of Meeting.

explanations.answer: His right earlobe and thumb and big toe
explanations.explanation: That's it. Leviticus 14:14 says the blood goes on “…the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.” Ear, thumb, toe. Me, I'm a stamper with a mustache, so I've got no earlobes and no toes, just a mustache doing all the work.

explanations.answer: His forehead and both of his hands
explanations.explanation: Not the forehead, and not both hands. The text says the blood goes on his right earlobe, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot (Leviticus 14:14). The oil on the head comes later, and it's the leftover oil (Leviticus 14:18). Three spots, all on the right side.

explanations.answer: His left ear and his left foot
explanations.explanation: You've got the right idea about ear and foot, but the side is flipped. Leviticus 14:14 names the right earlobe, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot. Left and right matter here. The thumb makes three spots, not two.

explanations.answer: To make atonement for him before the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Leviticus 14:18 says the rest of the oil goes on his head “…to make atonement for him before the LORD.” I'm not adding any extra reasons to that. The text gives the purpose, so I'll stand right there with it.

explanations.answer: To show he can serve as a priest
explanations.explanation: This verse doesn't say that. It says the oil goes on his head “…to make atonement for him before the LORD.” The person being cleansed isn't being made a priest here. The text gives atonement as the purpose, so that's what I go with.

explanations.answer: To heal what's left of his skin disease
explanations.explanation: By this point, the healing has already happened. The priest began the cleansing after he examined the person and found “…the skin disease of the afflicted person has healed…” (Leviticus 14:3). The oil on his head is “…to make atonement for him before the LORD.” (Leviticus 14:18). So the text gives atonement as the purpose, not healing.

Altar is right. Leviticus 14:20 says the priest offers the burnt offering “…on the altar, with the grain offering, to make atonement for him, and he will be clean.” That's the end of the first long list of offerings. The eighth day is a full one.

A table is a nice thought, but that's not where this offering goes. Leviticus 14:20 says the priest offers it “…on the altar…” The altar is where the burnt offering and grain offering go. A table is for me and my cookie boxes.
The lampstand isn't in this verse. The text says the priest offers the burnt offering and the grain offering “…on the altar…” A lampstand holds lamps, and this is an offering. The altar is the spot.

Lamb is right. Leviticus 14:21 says the poor person “…is to take one male lamb as a guilt offering…” Compare that with verse 10, where the other list has two male lambs and a ewe lamb. The poor person's list is shorter, but the guilt offering is still a lamb.
Goat is a reasonable guess, but the text says lamb. Leviticus 14:21 says he takes “…one male lamb as a guilt offering…” Goats don't show up anywhere in this chapter. Just the one lamb.

A bull is a big animal, and this list is the smaller one. Leviticus 14:21 says the poor person takes “…one male lamb as a guilt offering…” No bulls appear anywhere in this chapter. It's one lamb, nothing bigger.

Whichever he can afford is right. Leviticus 14:22 says, “…two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford…” The choice goes by what the person has. The text gives the poor person that room, and I like it.

The text doesn't say the priest chooses. Leviticus 14:22 says, “…two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford…” The measure is what the person can afford. The priest's part comes after, when he sacrifices the birds, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering (Leviticus 14:30-31).

Unblemished does show up in this chapter, but for the lambs (Leviticus 14:10). For the birds, verse 22 says, “…two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford…” That's the rule the text gives. It's about what he can afford.

It's actually false, friend. The poor person gets the same treatment. Leviticus 14:25 puts the blood “…on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.” and verse 28 puts the oil on “…the same places as the blood…” The offerings are smaller, but nothing gets skipped.

False is right. The poor person still gets the blood on the right earlobe, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot (Leviticus 14:25). Then the oil goes “…on the same places as the blood of the guilt offering.” (Leviticus 14:28). The list of offerings is smaller, but the steps are the same.
Come and tell the priest is right. Leviticus 14:35 says, “…the owner of the house shall come and tell the priest…” The owner doesn't handle it alone. He brings it to the priest.

No wall-tearing for the owner just yet. Leviticus 14:35 says he “…shall come and tell the priest…” The priest is the one who examines the mildew and gives the orders. Grabbing a hammer before the priest looks would be getting ahead of the instructions.

explanations.answer: Move his family out for good
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse says to move out for good. The owner “…shall come and tell the priest…” (Leviticus 14:35). The priest does the inspecting from there. Pack the moving boxes later, if ever.

Cleared is right, and it's smart. Leviticus 14:36 says, “The priest must order that the house be cleared before he enters it to examine the mildew…” Then comes the reason: “…so that nothing in the house will become unclean.” So everything comes out before the priest steps in. That's the kind of order I like, friend. Empty the house first, then look at the walls.

Washed is a fair guess, but this verse says the house is to be cleared. The priest “…must order that the house be cleared before he enters it to examine the mildew…” There's no washing before the inspection. The house gets emptied first.

Sealing does come up, but later. The priest closes the house up for seven days only after he examines it and finds the depressions (Leviticus 14:37-38). Before he goes in, the house is to be cleared (Leviticus 14:36). Order matters here.

explanations.answer: So nothing in it becomes unclean
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Leviticus 14:36 gives the reason: “…so that nothing in the house will become unclean.” The text states the reason plainly, so I don't need to add one. The house gets cleared first, then the priest goes in.

explanations.answer: So the priest has room to work
explanations.explanation: Room to work sounds sensible, but that's not the reason the text gives. Leviticus 14:36 says the house is cleared “…so that nothing in the house will become unclean.” I'd rather give you the reason the verse gives. It's about what's in the house.

explanations.answer: So the owner can count his goods
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions counting. It says the house is cleared “…so that nothing in the house will become unclean.” (Leviticus 14:36). That's the reason, and it's right there in the verse. A list of belongings isn't part of this scene.

explanations.answer: Pulled out and thrown outside the city
explanations.explanation: That's right. Leviticus 14:40 says he “…must order that the contaminated stones be pulled out and thrown into an unclean place outside the city.” The stones leave the house and the city. Imagine hauling that load, friend.

explanations.answer: Washed off and put back in place
explanations.explanation: The stones don't go back. Leviticus 14:40 says the contaminated stones are “…pulled out and thrown into an unclean place outside the city.” Then verse 42 says different stones are obtained to replace them. These ones are done.

explanations.answer: Piled up beside the house for a week
explanations.explanation: No piling beside the house. The text says the contaminated stones are “…pulled out and thrown into an unclean place outside the city.” (Leviticus 14:40). They go outside the city, not beside the house. The week was already used up when the house was closed (Leviticus 14:38).

It's false, friend. If the mildew comes back and spreads after the replastering, the text calls it “…a destructive mildew; the house is unclean.” (Leviticus 14:44). Then comes verse 45: “It must be torn down with its stones, its timbers, and all its plaster…” The text sends the house to be torn down, not scraped again.

False is right. When the mildew reappears and spreads, Leviticus 14:44 says, “…it is a destructive mildew; the house is unclean.” Then the house “…must be torn down with its stones, its timbers, and all its plaster…” (Leviticus 14:45). No second replastering is offered.

True. Leviticus 14:46 says, “Anyone who enters the house during any of the days that it is closed up will be unclean until evening.” The seven days start when the priest closes it up (Leviticus 14:38). So that's a house to stay out of.

It's true, friend. Leviticus 14:46 says, “Anyone who enters the house during any of the days that it is closed up will be unclean until evening.” That covers the days the priest has the house shut. Unclean until evening, not forever.
Clothes is right. Leviticus 14:47 says, “And anyone who sleeps in the house or eats in it must wash his clothes.” Sleeping in it or eating in it, both count. The laundry bill on this one is real.
Hand washing is a good habit, but that's not what this verse says. Leviticus 14:47 says anyone who sleeps in the house or eats in it “…must wash his clothes…” Clothes are the thing named here.

Feet are a natural guess, but the verse names something else. Leviticus 14:47 says anyone who sleeps in the house or eats in it “…must wash his clothes…” It's the clothes that get washed. Nobody mentions feet.
True. Leviticus 14:55 says this law covers “…mildew in clothing or in a house…” So clothing is named right alongside the house. The same law covers both.
It's true, friend. When God wraps up, Leviticus 14:55 includes “…mildew in clothing or in a house…” Clothing is named right there next to the house. The wrap-up covers more than walls.

explanations.answer: To tell when something is clean or unclean
explanations.explanation: That's it. Leviticus 14:57 says the law is “…to determine when something is clean or unclean.” Skin, mildew, a rash or a spot, it's all under that same purpose. The text gives the reason, and I'm happy to leave it there.

explanations.answer: To decide who can serve as a priest
explanations.explanation: That isn't the purpose the text gives. Leviticus 14:57 says the law is “…to determine when something is clean or unclean.” This chapter does have priests doing a lot of the work. But who serves as a priest isn't what the wrap-up is about.

explanations.answer: To set the days for the yearly feasts
explanations.explanation: No feast calendar in this wrap-up. The last verse says the law is “…to determine when something is clean or unclean.” (Leviticus 14:57). Days do matter in this chapter, like the seventh day and the eighth day. But those days belong to the cleansing, not to the feasts.
